opener.heading: Week 25: Juneteenth & Father's Day 🕊️
about: This week is about the people Azlyn belongs to and how she gets back to them. She cuts a chain of paper figures with one true sentence written on every body, clips the whole family along a string in the order they arrived, and sits on the floor while Joseph draws the street he grew up on. Then the week turns inward. Four faces on craft sticks for her own moods, your phone number sung to a tune she already knows, and a store aisle built out of dining chairs so she can practice being lost inside it. Each day puts the same question in front of her in a new shape: who are my people, and how do I find them again?

Three dates land inside the seven days. Juneteenth on Saturday gets a red picnic and the reason the food is red; Father's Day on Sunday gets the whole day, with Joseph on the floor and Azlyn holding the questions; the solstice on Monday gets the longest afternoon of the year, drawn out end to end along a strip of paper on the floor. Four things outlast the week: the paper chain along the wall at her height, June's pencil marks on the door frame beside January's, the number cards taped by the front door and inside the stroller, and the lamp post at the end of the street that this family now waits at. Tell whoever else has her about the lamp post.
azlyn: Where she sits among the people she belongs to. A paper figure for each of them with one true thing written on the body, then the same people clipped along a string in the order they arrived, Kreston at the near end.
A map starts at her own front door. Five places she knows, set near or far with a bottle cap, and the roads she turns onto to reach each one.
Evidence that she is changing. Pencil marks on the door frame beside January's, her palm laid inside her own January handprint, and baby trousers that stop at her knees.
Naming a mood out loud while she is inside it. Four faces on sticks standing in a mug within her reach, picked up by whoever's mood has moved, you included.
Her whole name, your phone number and three steps if she cannot see you. Stop, stand still, shout for Brooklyn by her name, run four times until her feet know it.
you: Playing you is how she works out what you do all day
Answer exactly what's asked about death, and no more
Maps are a major abstraction, and home is the way in
Children need external evidence of their own change
Holding two moods in one day is a real skill
Rehearsed safety knowledge survives panic; explained knowledge doesn't
Rehearsing a frightening scenario reduces the fear of it
shopping: A wallpaper offcut, or a long strip of newspaper, for the paper chain
Cereal boxes, 4 or 5, saved for card
Large cardboard boxes, 2, flattened (or a long roll of wrapping paper)
Paper cups and teaspoons, for freezing
January's handprint sheet, down off the wall
A measuring tape, or a length of string
Bottle caps or coins, 5, for the map
A coaster, or a plastic lid the size of Kreston's palm
Red fruit punch, or 4 hibiscus tea bags, or cranberry juice
Cans and boxes, 15–20 out of the cupboard (they go back after)
A saucepan and a wooden spoon
A toy phone, or the old handset with the battery taken out
A hat, scarf or bag belonging to each person in the house
A small bag or basket she can carry, and a purse with one coin in it
The box of outgrown baby clothes
opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 12 months this week. He walks, or he is days off it, drinks from an open cup with half of it down his front, and follows a one-step instruction often enough to be worth asking. He gets his own hat, his own card on the string and his own sheet at the end of the strip this week.

days.title: The Paper Family
days.prepTonight: Put four sheets of letter paper or a wallpaper offcut on the table with the crayons, and add strawberries, watermelon and a red drink to tomorrow's grocery list.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: The Daisy Chain That Keeps Breaking

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: You Be Me, I'll Be You

opening.title: Who Goes on the Chain
steps: Ask her who is in the family. Write the names in the order she says them and add nobody she has not named.
Read the list back. She will remember somebody, a grandparent or a cat, and they go on the bottom.
Count the names together and tell her that is how many people go on the chain at 9:15.

main.title: The Chain of People
materials: 4 sheets of letter paper, or a long strip of newspaper or wallpaper offcut
Your phone, to look at faces
steps: Tape the four sheets together along their short edges into one long strip, or use the offcut as it is.
Concertina-fold the strip, folds about as wide as her hand, one panel per name on this morning's list.
Draw half a person in pencil against the folded edge, arms running off both sides. The arms have to touch the folds or the chain comes apart.
Cut round your line while she watches, leaving the folds at the hands uncut. Open it out and hand her the row of people.
She gives every figure a face in crayon, with a photo of each person open on your phone so she draws from a real face.
Write on each body the exact thing that person does. Dad carries me on his shoulders. Kreston pulls my hair. Then tape the chain along the wall at her height.
main.tip: Write what the person does rather than what they are. Grandma keeps the cookies in the tin by the sink holds her for a week. Grandma is kind holds her for a second.

outside.title: The Daisy Chain That Keeps Breaking
paras: The daisies are up in the rough grass this week and the clover is thick in the lawn. Show her how to split a stem with a thumbnail and thread the next flower through, and switch to clover if the daisy stems are too short to work with. Her fingers cannot manage the split, so she picks and you thread, and the chain snaps every fourth flower. Make one long enough to go round her wrist.

days.infant: Kreston turned 1 on the fifth and follows a one-step instruction now. Hand him a paper offcut, say give it to Azlyn, and wait. He manages it half the time and the other half it goes in his mouth. Outside, let him pull at daisies with a whole fist: he grips the flower head, the stem stays in the ground, and he tries again thirty times.

second.title: You Be Me, I'll Be You
second.intro: Everybody swaps places until dinner. Azlyn takes Brooklyn's jobs and Brooklyn takes Azlyn's.
materials: 1 hat, scarf or bag belonging to each person
1 teddy, to stand in for anyone who isn't home
steps: Lay the hats, scarves and bags along the sofa, one per person, and let her choose who she is being. She will choose you.
Put on whatever belongs to her and carry her shoes, which will not go on your feet. She puts on yours and walks in them.
Give her the real job first: the fork drawer, one fork per person, laid round the table.
Take your turn as Azlyn. Ask for a snack in her words and her voice, and keep asking. Let her tell you no and mean it.
Sit teddy in the chair of whoever is out and put their hat on him. She decides what he does.
Photograph every person in the wrong hat while the swap is still running.
Swap back on purpose before dinner. Hats off, shoes off, names out loud.
second.tip: She copies the specific thing rather than the impression. The gesture that comes back at you is the one she has been studying.

alternatives: Swap the shoes only and leave it at that.
She feeds you your lunch, spoon by spoon, and you sit still for it.
Everyone draws everyone else as a stick figure holding one object.
outAgain: Grandparents or family, and take the paper chain to show whoever is on it
The park at the end of the road, on the shaded side
A walk to buy a popsicle and eat it before it gets home
The front step, naming everybody who walks past

aroundWorld.title: Freedom Days Everywhere 🕊️
paras: Countries mark the day they got free on different days. Juneteenth is June 19, the day in 1865 that Union soldiers reached Galveston, Texas, and made the end of slavery stick there. Trinidad and Jamaica hold Emancipation Day on August 1, with street parades that start before dawn. South Africa's freedom came later and from something else: Freedom Day on April 27 marks its first election open to every adult, and the end of apartheid.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Hibiscus makes a deep red drink, bissap in Senegal and sorrel in Jamaica, and it sits on Juneteenth tables across Texas. Steep two tea bags, cool it, sweeten it and let Azlyn pour. You want it again tomorrow.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: Freedom in Galveston arrived as a soldier reading an order out loud in the street. The news had reached Texas long before that, and it took troops standing there to make anybody act on it.

days.krestonPM: He gets a hat too. At 12 months he will lift it onto his own head, lose it over one eye and laugh at you laughing. Give him a rounded fork at the table while Azlyn lays it. A chair back and a fistful of your trouser leg get him across the room.

insight.headline: Playing you is how she works out what you do all day.
paras: You already hand her the real jobs, and this afternoon she takes the whole set: your shoes, your voice, the fork drawer. Copying is how a three-year-old gets inside a role she has only ever watched from underneath. She has seen you make a hundred decisions she could not follow, and putting your shoes on lets her run one of them from the inside. Expect the gesture that comes back at you to be exact, and expect it to be one you did not know you made. When she tells you no in your own words, she is finding out what the job feels like from your side of it.

days.safety: The scissors cut the chain and nothing else. Kreston is on his feet now and a table edge sits at his eye level, so nothing sharp gets left up there, not for a second and not while you answer the door. The scissors stay with you.

days.title: Before She Was Here
days.prepTonight: Cut a piece of cereal-box card for every person going on the line, and clear a shelf in the freezer for this afternoon's paper cups.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: Grown-Ups Who Used to Be Babies

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: How Many Azlyns Round the Tree

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: Up on Your Hip Along the Line

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: A Cool Bath and Two Books

opening.title: Grown-Ups Who Used to Be Babies
opening.need: your phone · 1 sheet of paper · 1 pencil.
steps: Find the oldest baby photograph on your phone of somebody now grown up, and show it to her without saying whose it is.
Let her guess, then tell her and watch her refuse to believe you.
Write down everybody she wants on the line, with a rough age beside each name. You need those numbers at 9:15.

main.title: Who Was Here First
materials: Card cut from a cereal box, 1 piece per person
Your phone, for photos to copy from
steps: Run the string across the room at your shoulder height and tape both ends down hard.
One card per person on the list. She draws each face in crayon with a photo open on your phone.
Write the name on every card in marker and the number of years underneath. Ninety-one takes some explaining.
Lay the cards on the floor and put them in order, oldest on the left. She argues about the middle.
She hands you the cards one at a time in that order and you clip them along the string. Kreston goes on last, at the near end.
Walk the whole line with her from the far end, saying each name and who came before them. Anybody who has died gets a card and a clothespin like everyone else.
main.tip: The line reads better from the far end. Everybody on it was here before her, and each one started where Kreston is standing now.

outside.title: How Many Azlyns Round the Tree
paras: Find the widest tree you can walk to and put her arms round it. She will not reach. Ask how many Azlyns it would take, then find out: she hugs the trunk, you mark where her fingertips stop, and she shuffles round. A tree that takes three of her was standing before Brooklyn was born. Take a spare length of the wool with you and wrap it round the trunk, then lay it out flat on the grass beside her so she can see the whole distance at once. Ask which of the people on this morning's line was already alive when the tree was thin enough for her to reach round.

days.infant: Kreston is 12 months and the youngest thing in the house. Hold him up to his own card and say his name; he will pat it. At the tree, stand him on the roots with both palms flat on the bark, which he has not felt before.

second.title: The Red Picnic
second.intro: Juneteenth tables run to red food and red drink. Azlyn builds the whole tray and nothing has to be cooked.
materials: Cherry tomatoes, 1 handful, quartered lengthways, and 1 red apple
Red fruit punch, or 2 hibiscus tea bags cooled and sweetened (cranberry juice substitutes for either)
Paper cups and teaspoons, for freezing
steps: She rinses the strawberries and pulls the green tops off.
You take the table knife. Watermelon into batons she can hold, every cherry tomato quartered lengthways, the apple sliced thin.
She lays it out on the tray, darkest red at one end and palest at the other.
Stir up the red drink, or steep the hibiscus bags in a mug out of reach and cool it in the fridge. She pours it into the cups.
Carry the tray outside into the shade and eat with fingers on the ground.
Tell her why the food is red: people have brought red drink and red food to this day for a hundred years, carried from West Africa.
Fill the leftover cups with the drink, stand a teaspoon upright in each and freeze them for tomorrow.
second.tip: A paper cup takes about four hours to freeze hard. Make twice as many as you need; tomorrow is hotter and there are two of them now.

alternatives: Red fruit straight out of the pint, no tray, no arranging.
Paint with a squashed strawberry instead of eating it.
Freeze the drink in an ice cube tray and drop the cubes into water.
Lay the tray out in stripes and eat one stripe at a time.
outAgain: The aquarium, dark the whole way round and out of the heat for an hour
The kiddie pool at home, if nobody can face the car
A shaded walk by the water, late enough that the path has cooled
The library, for the air conditioning as much as the books
A friend's garden, with the rest of the strawberries
days.krestonPM: At 12 months he drinks from an open cup with most of it down his front, which this afternoon counts as a service. Give him a shallow cup with one swallow in it, and quartered strawberry and quartered tomato only, on his own tray. He hands you a piece and takes it straight back.

insight.headline: Answer exactly what's asked about death, and no more.
paras: There is a card on the line for somebody who has died, and she will ask. Answer the question she asked and nothing past it. Where is he? wants a location, so give her one: he died, his body stopped working, he is buried at the church on the hill. Then stop and wait. She either goes back to lunch or asks the next question, which is the one worth answering. Three-year-olds take this in small doses over months and come back to it out of nowhere. Avoid lost, sleeping and gone away, because she takes all three at face value.

days.safety: Choking. Cherry tomatoes, grapes and watermelon chunks are round and the exact size of Kreston's airway at 12 months, so quarter everything lengthways and pick out the seeds before it reaches his tray. Run the string above his reach and take it down before bed, because a loop of string at toddler height is a strangulation risk.

days.title: Dad's Map
days.prepTonight: Flatten the biggest box in the house, or find a long length of wrapping paper, and put a second one aside for the afternoon. Yesterday's frozen cups come out of the freezer at half past three.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Map That Starts at Our Door

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: The Early Walk Before It Gets Hot

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Map of When Dad Was Little

opening.title: Where Dad Takes Her
steps: Ask her where Dad takes her. Write down the first five places she says, in her order.
Read them back. She will want to change the order, so renumber the list in front of her.
Tell her the five are going on a map this morning that starts at the front door.

main.title: The Map That Starts at Our Door
materials: 1 flattened cardboard box, or the back of a length of wrapping paper
5 bottle caps or coins, as place markers
1 coaster, or a plastic lid the size of Kreston's palm
steps: Tape the sheet down at all four corners so it stops sliding, and sit her in the middle of it.
She draws your front door in crayon in the middle, in its real color, the only thing on this map you place for her.
Hand her the five markers, one per place on the list. Near ones near the door, far ones at the edge.
She draws each place where its marker sits, then lifts the marker off. Write the name beside it in pencil so anybody else can read this.
Join them up with roads in marker. Ask which way you turn out of the door to reach each one.
Stand up and look down at it together, then photograph it from where you are standing.
main.tip: Her map has the ice cream shop the size of the park and the park the size of a stamp. Leave both.

outside.title: The Early Walk Before It Gets Hot
paras: Out by half past ten, and take the shortest of the five places on the map. Water, hats on both children, and shade at every stop. Stop at the corner she drew and let her tell you what comes next before you round it. She will get the order right and the distances wrong. Let her lead the walk home from that corner.

days.infant: Kreston is 12 months and wants to be on his feet. Let him walk part of the way holding one of your fingers and put him back in the stroller before he wilts. At home he gets the coaster, too big to go in his mouth, and he posts it under the edge of the cardboard and then hunts for it. Name whatever he points at on the walk, every time.

second.title: The Map of When Dad Was Little
second.intro: Joseph gets the floor. He has a whole place in his head that she has never seen.
materials: 1 second large sheet or flattened box
steps: Tape the second sheet down beside this morning's map so the two lie side by side.
Joseph draws his own front door in the middle, the one from when he was her age, in its real color.
Azlyn asks. Give her three to start: where did you sleep, where did you play, where did you get told off. He answers and draws, and she draws her version beside his.
He puts in five places of his own, the way she did this morning.
Walk both maps with a finger. Ask him what is still standing and what is gone.
He writes one sentence in pen along the bottom of each map and signs the second with the date.

Leave both maps down until bedtime. Then, if you used wrapping paper, fold the pair into the envelope and let her cover the front in crayon; if they are cardboard, stand them behind the closet and write the date on the back of each.
second.tip: Let her ask in her own order once the first three are used up. Her questions are stranger than yours.

alternatives: One map only, and it stays the one she drew this morning.
Joseph tells three stories from his old street and draws nothing.
Phone whoever else lived in that house and ask what they remember.
outAgain: A long walk with the stroller, Joseph pushing, going wherever he says
The shady side of the river, after four when the heat comes off it
A drive to somewhere he liked as a boy, with the windows down
The playground with the big slide, and he goes down it first
days.krestonPM: This is Joseph's day. At 12 months Kreston follows a one-step instruction, so bring it to Daddy is worth saying. Put him up on Joseph's shoulders for the last stretch home, both hands held, watching the branches.

insight.headline: Maps are a major abstraction, and home is the way in.
paras: A map asks Azlyn to accept that a flat line on cardboard stands for a road she has walked. That is a heavy ask at three, and it lands when the map starts somewhere her body knows. Children draw their own house and street years before they can read a printed map: the route from the door to the park is stored as a sequence of turns and landmarks. Drawing it turns that sequence into a picture she can look down on. Distance and scale stay wrong until about seven. The order of the places is the part she gets right, and order is what a map is for.

days.safety: Heat. The morning walk and the whole of Out Again are outdoors in the hottest week so far. A blanket or a thin cloth over the stroller traps heat instead of releasing it and the temperature underneath climbs fast, so shade the stroller by parking it, never by covering it. Water for everybody, sunscreen and hats on both children, and stops in real shade. A bottle cap is the width of Kreston's airway, so the five go back in the drawer the moment the map is finished.

days.title: The Longest Day
days.prepTonight: Get the box of outgrown baby clothes down and stand it by the door frame, and tape four sheets of paper end to end for the afternoon, or dig out a wallpaper offcut.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: The Trousers That Stop at Her Knees

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Day Drawn End to End

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Longest Bedtime of the Year

opening.title: The Trousers That Stop at Her Knees
opening.need: the box of outgrown baby clothes · a clear bit of floor.
steps: Tip the box out and sit in it with her. She picks out things she remembers wearing.
Let her try on whatever she wants. The trousers stop at her knees and the sleeves at her elbows.
Put two things aside for Kreston to grow into and stand the box by the door frame.

main.title: Back to the Door Frame
materials: 1 measuring tape, or a length of string
January's handprint sheet, down off the wall
The box of outgrown baby clothes
steps: Shoes off, heels against the door frame, everybody in turn. Mark each head in pencil and write the name and date beside it.
Find January's marks on the same frame. Measure the gap between hers with the tape or string.
Draw round her flat hand in pencil on the frame beside January's outline. Hers has grown past it on every finger.
January's handprint sheet off the wall and flat on the floor. She lays her palm inside her own January print and finds the gap round every finger.
Kreston's January print is on the same sheet beside hers. Open his hand over it and let her see how far past it he has gone in five months.
Hold the smallest thing in the box against him, then against Azlyn's back.
main.tip: Take the measurement where she can see it and say the number twice. A pencil mark six centimeters below her head is an argument she can put a hand on.

outside.title: Grass Taller Than Kreston
paras: Longest day of the year, and the grass on the roadsides is at full height. Find a patch that comes past her waist and stand Kreston in front of it. Let her push through ahead of you and wait for him to follow. Bring three seed heads home. Stand them in a jar on the windowsill where she can reach; they hold their shape for weeks. Ask which of the three came off the tallest stem, then hold it against her head and against yours. The roadsides reach full height this week and the city cuts them in July, so this is the one week the walk works.

days.infant: Kreston is 12 months, and the January print on that sheet was made while somebody held his fist open for it. He flattens his own hand now. In the long grass he grabs a fistful at face height and pulls, and finds out that grass is anchored and he is not.

second.title: The Day Drawn End to End
second.intro: Today runs longer than any other day this year, and she has no way to feel that. Laid out flat, it fills the floor.
materials: 4 sheets of paper taped end to end, or a wallpaper offcut
Your phone, with this morning's photographs on it
steps: Tape the strip down the middle of the floor. A sun coming up goes at the left end, a sun going down at the right.
Draw a line for lunch halfway along, then one more between that and each end. Four spaces, and the whole day fits inside them.
Start at the far left with the first thing she did. She will say breakfast, and the door frame comes second, because that is the bit she remembers.
One drawing per space, hers, in any order. Scroll this morning's photographs when she runs dry and let her find herself in them.
Write under each drawing what she says about it, word for word, in marker.
Leave the last space empty and tell her why: the light is still up at nine tonight, so there is day left to draw after dinner.
Go back at bedtime with the curtains open and let her fill it in with the sky still bright behind her.
second.tip: Draw nothing on it yourself. A strip with your hand on it records what you thought was worth keeping.

alternatives: Two spaces instead of four, and stop the strip at lunch.
Photograph the same corner of the garden at two, at five and at nine.
Tape the strip up the hallway wall at her height instead of down the floor.
outAgain: The riverside path, walked after five once the heat lifts off it
The park, still bright at nine tonight, so nothing has to be rushed
The top of the hill, to watch how long the sun takes to go down
The kiddie pool in the yard and nowhere at all
days.krestonPM: Give him his own sheet at the far end of the strip and one fat crayon, and expect the crayon in his mouth inside a minute. At 12 months he is working on standing up in the middle of the floor with nothing to hold, so keep him on the rug side of the strip.

insight.headline: Children need external evidence of their own change.
paras: Azlyn has no way of perceiving her own growth. She lives inside it, it happens at a rate no sense can pick up, and you're getting so big is a claim she has to take on trust. A pencil mark on a door frame is another matter. It sits outside her, it does not move, and the gap between January and today is a fact she can lay her hand flat against. Evidence she can put a hand on does the work the sentence cannot. The baby trousers that stop at her knees tell her something about Kreston as well as herself.

days.safety: The marker and the crayons sit at floor level all afternoon while Kreston walks around them, so the cap goes back on the pen between lines and the pen goes up on the table. Count the crayons back into the box at the end. Outside, the paving holds enough heat by mid-afternoon to burn bare feet, so put your hand flat on it first, and if the pool comes out you stay within arm's reach and tip it out before you go in.

days.title: Two Feelings in One Day
days.prepTonight: Put four paper plates, or a cereal box, on the table with the crayons and four craft sticks, and charge your phone.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: Photographing Every Face She Can Make

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Loud Corner and the Quiet Corner

opening.title: Photographing Every Face She Can Make
opening.need: your phone · a chair opposite yours.
steps: Sit facing her and pull the biggest sad face you can manage. She copies it without being asked; photograph her.
Work through happy, cross, scared, surprised and whatever she invents. One photo each, and let her look at every one.
Ask which of those faces she has already had this morning. Leave the photos open on your phone for 9:15.

main.title: The Face on a Stick
materials: 4 paper plates, or 4 circles cut from a cereal box
1 mug, to stand the four faces in
Your phone, for this morning's photos
steps: Scroll back through this morning's photos with her and pick four: happy, sad, cross, and one more that she names herself.
Cut four circles out of the cereal box while she watches, if you are not using plates.
She draws one face per circle in crayon with the photo beside her. Eyebrows do most of the work and she leaves them off until you point at them.
Tape a craft stick to the back of each face, low down, so the whole circle sits above her fist.
Ask her what the fourth face is called and write her word on the back of it. Wobbly is a real feeling.
Stand all four in a mug within her reach until bedtime. When your own mood changes, pick the matching one up and hold it in front of your face.
main.tip: Holding up the cross face at the moment you are cross teaches her more than any question about her feelings.

outside.title: The Faces Come With Us
paras: The four faces go out in her hand. Walk the usual block and stop at anything worth one: a dog behind a gate, a hedge being cut, somebody's sprinkler going, the crossing where the traffic is loud. She holds up whichever face fits and you hold up yours, and neither of you explains the choice. Ask her for one she has no stick for yet and write the word on the back of your own hand so it survives the walk. The four come home in the bag and go back in the mug until bedtime.

days.infant: Kreston is 12 months and reads faces off you well before he understands the words. Hold the happy face up beside your own and let him look between the two; he checks your real face for the answer, which is called social referencing. Give him a blank paper plate to bang, wear and post under the sofa.

second.title: The Loud Corner and the Quiet Corner
second.intro: Two corners go up at opposite ends of one room and stay up all afternoon.
steps: Build the loud corner first: saucepan, wooden spoon, and the empty laundry basket to climb into and drum on.
Quiet corner at the far end. Cushions on the floor, the blanket over a chair back for a low roof, the books stacked underneath and the flashlight on top.
Show her both and say one sentence about each. She goes where she goes.
Get into the loud corner with her once and bang the saucepan harder than she does.
Later, lie down in the quiet corner on your own without inviting her. She turns up.
When she crosses from one to the other, say what you saw. You were banging, and now you want the dark. Leave out the question about why.
Leave both corners standing until bedtime, and read the last two books in the quiet one.
second.tip: She spends twenty minutes in the loud corner and four in the quiet one, then flips it tomorrow. The ratio is hers.

alternatives: Loud corner only, out in the yard, with every pan in the cupboard.
Quiet corner only, if the morning has already been too much.
A cardboard box with the blanket over it instead of the chair.
Flashlight and books under the dining table, and stay there.
outAgain: Swimming, and the coolest hour of the whole week
The kiddie pool at home if the pool is packed with the holiday crowd
A splash pad or a fountain, with a change of clothes in the bag
The hose on the grass at home, and nothing else planned
days.krestonPM: He has swimming too. At 12 months he can stand on the shallow step holding the rail, and he lets go without meaning to, so stay within one arm's length for the whole session. Twenty minutes is plenty in a cool pool. At home he finds the loud corner on his own and picks up the wooden spoon.

insight.headline: Holding two moods in one day is a real skill.
paras: Azlyn spent the morning laughing and the afternoon furious about a sock. At three she runs one feeling at a time at full volume, and the switch between them looks alarming from outside. The skill she is building is tolerating the change: learning that the cross feeling ends and does not swallow the rest of the day. Naming states out loud while she is inside them, and keeping a place in the house for each one, hands her the words and the room. A child who can put a word on a feeling comes out of it faster, and she picks the words up by hearing them used on her while she is still inside one.

days.safety: The scissors cut the four circles and then leave the room. Loose craft sticks stay off the floor while Kreston is down there, because they splinter and they fit down his throat. He gets a paper plate and nothing thinner than that. The scissors stay with you. Swimming this afternoon. Both children stay within arm's reach in the water at all times, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands.

days.title: What She Knows By Heart
days.prepTonight: Cut four pieces of card out of a cereal box, take the battery out of the old handset, and put the chalk by the door with her shoes.

opening.title: Her Name, All of It
steps: Ask her name. She gives you the first one. Ask for the rest and supply whatever she misses.
Write the whole thing out big and let her put a finger on each part while you say it: first, middle, last.
Tell her Brooklyn has a whole name too, and say it. She has never heard it. Do Joseph's and Kreston's.

main.title: The Number She Sings
materials: Card cut from a cereal box, 4 pieces
1 toy phone, or the real handset with the battery out
steps: Pick a tune she knows the whole way through. Twinkle Twinkle takes ten digits without much shoving.
Sing your phone number to it three times before you ask her to join in. Expect the middle three digits to go missing for a week.
Write the number across each of the four cards in marker, big, and let her fill the rest with crayon.
Tape one card by the front door at her height, one in the stroller, one in her bag, and keep the fourth for whoever else has her.
Give her the dead handset. She presses the buttons and says the number to whoever she has decided is at the other end.
Record her singing it on your phone. Somebody else may need to hear how she sings it.
main.tip: Sing it rather than reciting it. A tune carries a string of digits into long-term memory, which is why you still know the alphabet in order.

outside.title: The Lamp Post We Meet At
paras: Walk out of the front door and stop at the first fixed thing on the street: a lamp post, a mailbox, the corner of the garden wall. Put her hand flat on it. From today, that is where anybody in this family who gets separated waits. Walk to it from the door three times, then point it out from further up the street. Say the rule in the same five words every time, so she ends up with one sentence. Then tell everybody else who has her: the grandparents, the neighbor, whoever collects her from preschool. A meeting place only works when every adult in her life knows the same one. Chalk a mark at the foot of it before you walk home, low enough that she finds it tomorrow.

days.infant: Kreston is 12 months and copying sound long before he has words. He will hum the shape of your phone number back at you months before a single digit is right. Sit him in the stroller while you tape his card inside, let him pull it off once, then tape it back where he cannot get a fingernail under.

second.title: Shoes On and Out the Door
second.intro: You walk the same route out of the house until her feet know it. Run it as a race and she will do it four times without being asked twice.
materials: 1 teddy, as the thing you leave behind
steps: Walk the route once with no timer. Shoes on at the door, out, along the sidewalk, stop at the lamp post from this morning.
Chalk a circle at the foot of it on the house side, big enough for her to stand inside with both feet and well back from the curb.
Give her the rule once: shoes on, straight out, stand in the circle, wait. Skip the explanation of what it is for.
Now time it. Three runs, and tell her the number after each one. She will want it faster every time.
On the third run, put teddy on the floor halfway to the door and say his name as you pass. She does not go back. Nobody goes back inside for anything.
Fourth run under real conditions: your arms are full of Kreston, so this one is walked rather than raced, and you are out of the door before she is.
Finish with her chalking whatever she likes round the circle.
second.tip: Stop the moment it stops being a game. A drill she enjoyed gets run again next month. One that frightened her gets refused.

alternatives: The route walked once at her pace, with no timing at all.
Chalk the whole way from the door to the lamp post in arrows.
She teaches teddy the rule and says it out loud in her own words.
outAgain: The library, and the coolest room she will sit in all day
Indoor playground, indoors and out of the sun
The park after six, once the shade has reached the swings
A walk to the mailbox with a letter she posts herself
days.krestonPM: Take him to the library and put him down. At 12 months he cruises the picture book shelf and pulls every third book onto the floor, and the staff have seen it before. Let Azlyn choose two for him and carry them to the desk. During the drill he is in your arms.

insight.headline: Rehearsed safety knowledge survives panic; explained knowledge doesn't.
paras: Azlyn can recite that she waits at the lamp post and still stand frozen on the sidewalk when it happens for real. Under stress, the part of memory that holds explanations drops out first, and what stays is whatever her body has already done. Rehearsal moves the knowledge into that second store. Four runs today, four more next month, and the way out of the door becomes something her feet know rather than something she was told once in the kitchen. The tune does the same job for the number. Adults get trained this way for the same reason, and a three-year-old takes it in the same way.

days.safety: The drill itself. She never goes back inside for anything, and she is never taught to hide. Clear the route first, check the sidewalk and the road at the lamp post, and stop the moment it frightens her. She stops at the circle by the wall, never at the curb, and you are out of the door before her and on the curb side every time. On the fourth run Brooklyn's arms are full of Kreston, so Azlyn walks that one on her own, with the timer off.

days.title: If She Can't See You
days.prepTonight: Stand a bag of cans by the dining chairs, and check yesterday's name-and-number card is still in her bag.

opening.title: Spotting Who Works There
steps: Pull up a photo of the store you use and look at it together over breakfast.
Ask her who works there and how you would know. Aprons, a badge with a name on it, standing behind the register.
Tell her the person with the badge is who she talks to if she cannot see you. Say it once and let it sit.

main.title: Stop, Stand Still, Shout
materials: 15–20 cans and boxes from the cupboard
1 roll masking tape, for the aisle floor
1 sheet of paper and 1 marker, for the name badge
1 teddy, as the person behind the register
steps: Tape two long lines down the floor and stand the chairs along them, backs to the aisle. Drape the blanket over the backs so she cannot see across, and set the cans and boxes in one low row along the seats.
Write a name across the paper in marker, teddy's name will do, tape it to his front and sit him at the end of the aisle. That is the badge she is looking for.
Walk the aisle with her, then step round the end and out of her sight.
She practices three things in this order: stop walking, stay exactly where she is, shout for Brooklyn by her name. Not Mommy. In a store full of mothers, the actual name is what turns a head.
Run it three times: appear at once on the first, count to five on the second, count to fifteen on the third.
Last run, she goes to teddy instead of shouting and tells him her own name and Brooklyn's whole name, both learned yesterday.
main.tip: She will shout for you in a whisper the first time. Get her doing it at full volume in the house today.

outside.title: Bees on the Lavender
paras: The lavender is in full flower this week and it will be loud. Find a bush, in a front yard, a parking lot bed or the corner of the park, and stand close enough to hear it. Count the bees on one bush, then move to the next and see whether the number holds. Tell her once that a bee working a flower has no interest in a person standing still. Rub a head of lavender between your fingers and hold them under her nose.

days.infant: Kreston is 12 months and will follow Azlyn down the aisle on his feet, taking cans off the seats as he passes. At the lavender, hold him level with the flowers to watch a bee move stem to stem.

second.title: The List She Can Read
second.intro: Everything she practiced on the taped floor this morning walks into a real shop.
steps: Cut one sheet of paper into five pieces. You hold the scissors.
Say the five things you need out loud, and she draws one on each piece.
Tape the five pieces in a row down the second sheet so the whole list holds together in one hand.
Pack the bag with her: the list, the purse with the coin, and yesterday's name-and-number card taped flat inside.
Walk to the store at half past two with the bag over her shoulder and the list in her fist.
She finds all five things and puts them in the basket herself, marking each picture with a crayon as it goes in.
She hands the coin over for one item at the register and puts the change back in the purse herself.

alternatives: Three pictures, one small store, ten minutes, home.
Run the aisles again at home and skip the real store.
Draw the list today and shop tomorrow, when it is cooler.
outAgain: The grocery store, with her list and her bag, run as the outing itself
The corner store for milk and one thing she picks
The park afterwards, with something cold out of the store
A friend's garden, if the store trip takes ten minutes
days.krestonPM: He rides in the cart seat with the strap done up, facing Azlyn, and he holds one item for the whole store. At 12 months he follows a one-step instruction, so try give it to the lady at the register. Nothing goes in his mouth off a shelf, and the strap goes on before you reach the first aisle.

insight.headline: Rehearsing a frightening scenario reduces the fear of it.
paras: Talking about getting lost sounds like the thing that plants the fear. It runs the other way round. A frightening idea with no script attached grows in the dark; the same idea with three practiced steps turns into a job she knows how to do. She has now been lost in an aisle made of dining chairs and got herself found, three times, in a room where you were nine feet away. Rehearsal leaves her less to be frightened of and gets her moving sooner when it happens. Keep your tone flat and ordinary and she takes it as one more thing she can do.

days.safety: The parking lot and the lure. She never walks outside to look for Brooklyn, and she never goes with an adult who asks her to come and help find her mom. Anybody who wants to help fetches a member of staff and stays put. Hand or cart from the store door to the car, nothing left in a parked car in this heat, and the scissors stay with you. Nothing in the aisle gets stacked above Kreston's head height. He hauls himself upright on chair backs, so the cans stay in one row along the seats and the blanket is the only thing higher than he is.
